tldr: In latent action models that learn actions self-supervised from video, this robot world model introduces skeleton supervision and cross-modal swap reconstruction to disentangle robot kinematic motion from environmental visual dynamics, significantly improving control adherence and visual quality.

(B) World model pre-training incorporating branch dropout. (C) Training a lightweight adapter mapping real robot actions to the kinematic latent space, and the inference generation flow.
overview:
A "world model" predicts how the environment evolves in response to a robot's actions. It has attracted significant attention as a foundation for simulation and policy evaluation. Recently, methods that extract visual transitions from large amounts of unlabeled video as "latent actions" have become popular. However, conventional reconstruction-driven learning suffers from a major issue: the robot's own end-effector motion gets tangled up with environmental dynamics, such as objects rolling or deforming, within the latent representation. Consequently, when mapping real robot control commands (actions) into this latent space, the correspondence becomes ambiguous, making it difficult to simulate intended behaviors accurately.

To address this, the authors propose "SkeLAM," a method that leverages robot skeleton images as supervisory signals to cleanly disentangle latent actions into a geometric "kinematic component" representing the robot's own movement and a "residual component" capturing complementary environmental changes. In addition, they introduce "cross-modal swap reconstruction," where the kinematic representation derived from an RGB encoder can be swapped with one derived from skeletons while still correctly reconstructing the original RGB frame. This forces the decoder to treat both representations as interchangeable kinematic instructions. During world model training, "branch dropout" is applied, conditioning the model to adapt to inference-time scenarios where future residual information is absent (set to zero).

In experiments on DROID, a real-world scale robot manipulation dataset, SkeLAM reduces end-effector average displacement error (ADE) by 19.5% and improves perceptual quality (LPIPS) by 11.1% compared to existing latent action world models such as DreamDojo. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer by extracting latent actions from human demonstration videos to generate robot rollouts, and show that success rates predicted inside the world model faithfully match evaluations on real robots.
contributions: Proposed a framework that explicitly decomposes latent actions into a kinematic component grounded in robot motion via skeleton supervision and a residual component retaining environmental dynamics.
Introduced cross-modal swap reconstruction by interchanging skeleton- and RGB-derived kinematic representations during decoding, establishing functional interchangeability at the generator level.
Enabled high-precision future prediction at inference using only the current frame and real robot actions through branch dropout and a lightweight adapter.
Demonstrated zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer and strong correlation with real robot policy evaluations, in addition to high-accuracy future rollout prediction on DROID.

sections.heading: Why do we need to separate kinematic motion from environmental changes in latent actions?
sections.summary: Conventional approaches that learn latent actions from video mix robot motion with object responses, complicating correspondence with control commands. This paper proposes SkeLAM, which explicitly separates and grounds kinematic components using skeleton images to achieve a highly accurate, controllable world model.
sections.details:
A robot world model is a simulator that predicts how the environment evolves in response to given actions. It is essential for model-based reinforcement learning and safe policy evaluation. However, collecting real-robot datasets with action labels is costly, which has popularized learning "latent actions" from frame transitions in unlabeled videos in a self-supervised manner.

Yet, when latent actions are trained simply to reconstruct the next frame, the arm movement of the robot and environmental responses—like objects rolling or slipping upon contact—become blended into a single latent vector. For example, even if the arm moves in the exact same way, the resulting frame looks very different depending on whether it makes contact with an object. Because of this entanglement, scene-dependent noise disrupts learning when subsequently trying to map real control commands (such as joint angles or end-effector velocities) onto the latent action space.

To tackle this, the researchers turned to the "robot skeleton," which contains no visual appearance of surrounding objects. The latent representation extracted from consecutive RGB frames is decomposed into two parts: a "kinematic latent" anchored to the physical robot motion by the skeleton, and a "residual latent" covering background and object changes. Furthermore, by performing "cross-modal swap reconstruction"—reconstructing RGB frames while swapping the RGB-derived kinematic representation with the skeleton-derived one—the generative decoder is forced to treat both as identical kinematic directives.

In evaluations on the DROID dataset, this approach cuts end-effector average displacement error (ADE) by 19.5% and improves LPIPS by 11.1% compared to prior methods, successfully achieving both motion compliance and visual realism.

sections.heading: The evolution of world models and latent action learning, and where SkeLAM stands
sections.summary: We review previous work on direct-action-conditioned and latent-action-based world models. While traditional latent action models are vulnerable to distractors and confounding, SkeLAM uses geometric prior knowledge from skeletons to cleanly structure motion representations.
sections.details:
Related work broadly spans three main areas:

- **Action-conditioned robot world models**: Recent studies (such as Ctrl-World and IRASim) feed real robot actions into diffusion models or Transformers to predict future frames. Some methods directly take skeleton sequences or 3D renderings as inputs, but this introduces the constraint of requiring complete skeleton plans or geometric models even at inference time.
- **Latent action learning from videos**: Approaches pre-trained on large-scale video (such as DreamDojo) face challenges from environmental distractors and ambiguous mappings. While some have tried using optical flow to isolate agent movement, interactions with the environment still remain tangled in the latent space.
- **Structured action representations**: Works are exploring physical priors in action spaces, such as skill quantization, graph neural networks, and trajectory diffusion models.

SkeLAM's uniqueness lies in the fact that "skeleton information is only used as privileged supervision (a scaffold) during representation learning, while inference operates purely on RGB images and regular robot actions." Because there is no need to supply a continuous skeleton sequence at test time, it plugs directly into existing robot control interfaces.

sections.heading: Skeleton-grounded kinematic latents and action-driven world model generation
sections.summary: Latent actions are decomposed into kinematic and residual components, structuring the kinematic space with skeleton loss and swap reconstruction. The world model is trained with branch dropout, enabling future video generation from real robot actions via a lightweight adapter.
sections.details:
The SkeLAM training pipeline consists of two primary stages: latent action learning and world model learning.

### 3.1 Skeleton-Grounded Latent Action Model (SkeLAM)
First, from consecutive RGB frames $(o_t, o_{t+1})$, the model extracts a kinematic component $z_{\mathrm{kin},t}^{\mathrm{rgb}} \in \mathbb{R}^{32}$ and a residual component $z_{\mathrm{res},t}^{\mathrm{rgb}} \in \mathbb{R}^{32}$. Concurrently, from corresponding robot skeleton frames $(s_t, s_{t+1})$, it extracts a skeleton kinematic component $z_{\mathrm{kin},t}^{\mathrm{ske}} \in \mathbb{R}^{32}$.

Two core mechanisms are introduced here:
- **Skeleton Grounding**: A pre-trained, frozen skeleton decoder takes $z_{\mathrm{kin},t}^{\mathrm{rgb}}$ as input to reconstruct the next skeleton image $s_{t+1}$. An alignment loss also maximizes cosine similarity between $z_{\mathrm{kin},t}^{\mathrm{rgb}}$ and $z_{\mathrm{kin},t}^{\mathrm{ske}}$ in the latent space. This confines the RGB-derived kinematic component strictly to the robot's physical articulation.
- **Cross-Modal Swap Reconstruction**: When the RGB decoder restores the next RGB frame $o_{t+1}$, the kinematic input $z_{\mathrm{kin},t}^{\mathrm{rgb}}$ is swapped with the paired skeleton kinematic representation $z_{\mathrm{kin},t}^{\mathrm{ske}}$. By training the decoder to reconstruct the image correctly when combined with the original residual $z_{\mathrm{res},t}^{\mathrm{rgb}}$, RGB-derived and skeleton-derived kinematic representations become fully interchangeable for the decoder.

### 3.2 Action-Conditioned World Model Training and Inference
In the world model (backed by Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B), the kinematic and residual components are projected via separate MLP conditioning branches.

A vital design here is **Branch Dropout**. At inference time, future frames are unavailable, so the residual component $z_{\mathrm{res}}$ cannot be computed. During world model training, four conditions are randomly sampled: "keep both," "keep kinematic only (drop residual)," "keep residual only," and "drop both." This conditions the world model to make stable future predictions using only the kinematic branch when the residual is missing (set to zero).

Finally, a lightweight MLP adapter is trained via regression to map real robot actions $a_t$ (7-dimensional relative translation, rotation, and gripper state) to $z_{\mathrm{kin},t}^{\mathrm{rgb}}$. Because the kinematic component has been geometrically purified by the skeleton, learning this mapping is straightforward. At inference, given the current frame $o_t$ and an action sequence, the adapter provides kinematic latents, the residual branch is zeroed out, and the world model generates high-quality future video sequences non-autoregressively in one pass.

sections.heading: Validation on real robot data: Kinematic accuracy, visual quality, and policy evaluation
sections.summary: On the DROID dataset, SkeLAM significantly outperforms existing world models in trajectory accuracy and image quality. Its effectiveness is further corroborated by linear probing of representations, zero-shot motion transfer, and offline policy evaluation.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted primarily on the large-scale real-robot manipulation dataset DROID (Franka Panda arm), supplemented by AgiBot data. The prediction horizon is 12 frames (roughly 0.8 seconds at 15 FPS).

### 4.1 Experimental Setup and Baselines
Baselines include latent-action-based models like DreamDojo and CD-LAM, direct-action-conditioned models like Ctrl-World, IRASim, and Cosmos-Predict2.5, and geometry-guided models like OSCAR. Comprehensive evaluation is conducted using end-effector Average Displacement Error (ADE in pixels), direction consistency ($\mathrm{F1}_{\mathrm{dir}}$), and visual quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS).

### 4.2 World Model Prediction Accuracy and Ablations
In quantitative evaluation, SkeLAM achieved the top score across 7 out of 8 metrics among action-conditioned models. In particular, compared with DreamDojo, it reduced end-effector ADE by 19.5% and perceptual error LPIPS by 11.1% (from 0.1473 down to 0.1310). Compared with Ctrl-World, which directly takes raw actions, it significantly improved ADE from 42.96 px to 41.15 px, and LPIPS from 0.4029 to 0.1310.

Ablation studies demonstrated that omitting any proposed module degrades performance:
- Removing skeleton supervision caused ADE to deteriorate sharply from 41.15 px to 64.59 px.
- Removing swap reconstruction worsened ADE to 66.74 px, and the correlation coefficient for motion magnitude dropped drastically.
- Training with residual latents set to zero from the start maintained visual quality but degraded ADE to 43.37 px, revealing that modeling environmental dynamics through residuals indirectly benefits kinematic prediction.

### 4.3 Latent Representation Analysis
In linear probing experiments predicting end-effector motion from frozen latents, the 32-dimensional kinematic latent alone achieved virtually identical accuracy (EEF MAE $5.99 \times 10^{-3}$) to the full 64-dimensional concatenation of kinematic and residual latents. In intervention tests where mismatched skeleton latents were fed to the RGB decoder, reconstruction MAE jumped by 11.67%, proving that the decoder responds sensitively to kinematic misalignments.

### 4.4 Zero-Shot Human-to-Robot Motion Transfer
By extracting latent actions with the RGB encoder from human hand manipulation videos in the UniSkill dataset and pairing them with an initial robot frame, SkeLAM generated future robot arm motions following human gestures (such as "pushing a towel" or "pulling a tissue") zero-shot, without any additional fine-tuning. In contrast, DreamDojo froze mid-rollout and failed to move the robot.

### 4.5 Real-Robot Policy Evaluation (RoboArena)
Open-loop execution videos of 7 policies (based on Pi0 and PaliGemma) were generated on SkeLAM, and human evaluators scored task success. Evaluating correlation with real-robot execution success rates, Cosmos-Predict2.5 produced a negative Spearman rank correlation of $\rho = -0.1980$, whereas SkeLAM achieved $\rho = 0.5347$ and a Pearson correlation of $r = 0.6091$, demonstrating faithful reproduction of real robot performance rankings.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook: Extending toward closed-loop policy evaluation
sections.summary: SkeLAM disentangles latent actions into kinematic and residual components using skeletons, delivering a controllable, high-fidelity world model. Future research will explore moving beyond open-loop action replay to extended, interactive closed-loop simulations.
sections.details:
This work presented SkeLAM, a world model that leverages skeleton information to structure latent actions into robot kinematics and residual dynamics. By pairing cross-modal swap reconstruction with branch dropout, the system eliminates the need for auxiliary geometric inputs during inference, achieving precise motion adherence alongside high-fidelity simulation using standard robot actions.

As a future direction, the authors highlight expanding beyond the open-loop replay of pre-recorded actions evaluated here toward "closed-loop policy evaluation," where generated frames are fed back to the policy in real time to determine subsequent actions. Understanding how prediction errors compound over extended rollouts and affect policy decision-making will be key to establishing world models as authentic simulators.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation details, data processing, and extra qualitative results
sections.summary: Details on dataset preprocessing (DROID, AgiBot), training schedules, metric calculations, and additional qualitative predictions in kitchen scenes.
sections.details:
### Datasets and Preprocessing
Stage 1 latent action learning was trained on 60,000 clips from DROID, followed by world model pre-training and adaptation on 45,358 clips. Images are letterboxed to $240 \times 320$ preserving aspect ratios, and center-cropped to $480 \times 640$ during world model training. Robot action data consists of a 7-dimensional vector representing relative translation, rotation vector, and gripper state in the base frame.

### Training Details
The VAE backbone utilizes a 16-layer Transformer with a patch size of $16 \times 16$ and hidden dimension of 1024. The world model is based on Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B, trained across 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs in roughly 2 days. Training follows a phased curriculum, beginning with skeleton pre-training and sequentially activating grounding loss, alignment loss, and swap loss.

### Additional Qualitative Evaluation
Even in visually cluttered kitchen scenes (Figure F9), SkeLAM is not thrown off by lighting shifts or background distractions, accurately simulating gripper open/close states and end-effector trajectories during grasping maneuvers compared to alternative approaches.

captions.F9: Additional qualitative comparisons in kitchen environments. Even with complex backgrounds and heavy visual textures, SkeLAM (Ours) accurately reproduces end-effector target positions and trajectories without arm collapse.

takeaways: When applying latent action models to robot control, relying solely on reconstruction loss is insufficient; explicitly disentangling "kinematics" from "environmental changes" via geometric cues like skeletons is highly effective.

Using privileged skeleton signals strictly during representation learning, alongside decoder swap training and branch dropout, enables a practical pipeline driven by ordinary action commands at inference.
A purified kinematic latent space serves as a viable cross-domain interface for zero-shot motion transfer across distinct physical embodiments, such as human hands to robot arms.
limitations: Evaluation is predominantly confined to open-loop rollouts (replaying pre-recorded actions), leaving long-horizon closed-loop simulation—where generated frames feed back into policy decisions—unexplored.
Generating skeleton supervision requires pre-existing robot kinematic models (URDFs) and accurate camera extrinsic parameters within the training dataset.
On the AgiBot dataset, while SSIM improved, gains in LPIPS and ADE were not as uniform as on DROID, indicating that effectiveness can vary depending on robot embodiment and data diversity.
